{{Technical|date=April 2025}}
Within [[mathematics]], an ''N''×''N'' '''Euclidean random matrix''' Â is defined with the help of an arbitrary deterministic function ''f''('''r''', '''r'''′) and of ''N'' points {'''r'''<sub>i</sub>} randomly distributed in a region ''V'' of ''d''-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]. The element A<sub>ij</sub> of the matrix is equal to ''f''('''r'''<sub>i</sub>, '''r'''<sub>j</sub>): A<sub>ij</sub> = ''f''('''r'''<sub>i</sub>, '''r'''<sub>j</sub>).

== History ==
Euclidean [[Random matrix|random matrices]] were first introduced in 1999.<ref name=mezard99>{{Cite journal | last1 = Mezard | first1 = M.| last2 = Parisi | first2 = G.| last3 = Zee | first3 = A. | title = Spectra of euclidean random matrices | doi = 10.1016/S0550-3213(99)00428-9 | journal = Nuclear Physics B | volume = 559 | issue = 3 | pages = 689–701| year = 1999 |arxiv = cond-mat/9906135 |bibcode = 1999NuPhB.559..689M | s2cid = 3020186}}</ref> They studied a special case of functions ''f'' that depend only on the distances between the pairs of points: ''f''('''r''', '''r'''′) = ''f''('''r''' - '''r'''′) and imposed an additional condition on the diagonal elements A<sub>ii</sub>,

:A<sub>ij</sub> = ''f''('''r'''<sub>i</sub> - '''r'''<sub>j</sub>) - u δ<sub>ij</sub>Σ<sub>k</sub>''f''('''r'''<sub>i</sub> - '''r'''<sub>k</sub>),
 
motivated by the physical context in which they studied the matrix.
A [[Euclidean distance matrix]] is a particular example of Euclidean random matrix with either ''f''('''r'''<sub>i</sub> - '''r'''<sub>j</sub>) = |'''r'''<sub>i</sub> - '''r'''<sub>j</sub>|<sup>2</sup> or ''f''('''r'''<sub>i</sub> - '''r'''<sub>j</sub>) = |'''r'''<sub>i</sub> - '''r'''<sub>j</sub>|.<ref name=bogo03>{{Cite journal | last1 = Bogomolny | first1 = E. | last2 = Bohigas | first2 = O. | last3 = Schmit | first3 = C. | doi = 10.1088/0305-4470/36/12/341 | title = Spectral properties of distance matrices | journal = Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General | volume = 36 | issue = 12 | pages = 3595–3616 | year = 2003 |arxiv = nlin/0301044 |bibcode = 2003JPhA...36.3595B | s2cid = 15199709 }}</ref>

For example, in many biological networks, the strength of interaction between two nodes depends on the physical proximity of those nodes. Spatial interactions between nodes can be modelled as a Euclidean random matrix, if nodes are placed randomly in space.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Muir|first1=Dylan|last2=Mrsic-Flogel|first2=Thomas|title=Eigenspectrum bounds for semirandom matrices with modular and spatial structure for neural networks|journal=Phys. Rev. E|date=2015|volume=91|issue=4|article-number=042808|doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.91.042808|pmid=25974548|url=http://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.91.042808|bibcode=2015PhRvE..91d2808M}}</ref><ref name="Grilli2015">{{cite journal|last1=Grilli|first1=Jacopo|last2=Barabás|first2=György|last3=Allesina|first3=Stefano|title=Metapopulation Persistence in Random Fragmented Landscapes|journal=PLOS Computational Biology|volume=11|issue=5|year=2015|article-number=e1004251|issn=1553-7358|doi=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1004251|pmid=25993004|bibcode=2015PLSCB..11E4251G|pmc=4439033 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Properties ==
Because the positions of the points {'''r'''<sub>i</sub>} are random, the matrix elements A<sub>ij</sub> are random too. Moreover, because the ''N''×''N'' elements are completely determined by only ''N'' points and, typically, one is interested in ''N''≫''d'', strong correlations exist between different elements.

[[File:Fig sinc.png|thumb|340px|alt=Example 1 | Example of the probability distribution of eigenvalues Λ of the Euclidean random matrix generated by the function ''f''('''r''', '''r'''′) = sin(''k''<sub>0</sub>ǀ'''r'''-'''r'''′ǀ)/(''k''<sub>0</sub>ǀ'''r'''-'''r'''′ǀ), with ''k''<sub>0</sub> = 2π/λ<sub>0</sub>. The Marchenko-Pastur distribution (red) is compared with the result of numerical diagonalization of a set of randomly generated matrices of size ''N''×''N''. The density of points is ρλ<sub>0</sub><sup>3</sup> = 0.1.]]

=== Hermitian Euclidean random matrices ===

[[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian]] Euclidean random matrices appear in various physical contexts, including supercooled liquids,<ref name=grigera03>{{Cite journal | last1 = Grigera | first1 = T. S. | last2 = Martín-Mayor | first2 = V. | last3 = Parisi | first3 = G. | last4 = Verrocchio | first4 = P. | title = Phonon interpretation of the 'boson peak' in supercooled liquids | doi = 10.1038/nature01475 | journal = Nature | volume = 422 | issue = 6929 | pages = 289–292 | year = 2003 | pmid =  12646916|bibcode = 2003Natur.422..289G | s2cid = 4393962 }}</ref> [[Phonon|phonons]] in disordered systems,<ref name=amir10>{{Cite journal | last1 = Amir | first1 = A. | last2 = Oreg | first2 = Y. | last3 = Imry | first3 = Y. | title = Localization, Anomalous Diffusion, and Slow Relaxations: A Random Distance Matrix Approach | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.105.070601 | journal = Physical Review Letters | volume = 105 | issue = 7 | year = 2010 | pmid =  20868026|arxiv = 1002.2123 |bibcode = 2010PhRvL.105g0601A | article-number=070601| s2cid = 42664610 }}</ref> and waves in random media.<ref name=skipetrov11>{{Cite journal | last1 = Skipetrov | first1 = S. E. | last2 = Goetschy | first2 = A. | doi = 10.1088/1751-8113/44/6/065102 | title = Eigenvalue distributions of large Euclidean random matrices for waves in random media | journal = Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical | volume = 44 | issue = 6 | article-number = 065102 | year = 2011 |arxiv = 1007.1379 |bibcode = 2011JPhA...44f5102S | s2cid = 119152955 }}</ref>

''Example 1:'' Consider the matrix Â generated by the function ''f''('''r''', '''r'''′) = sin(''k''<sub>0</sub>|'''r'''-'''r'''′|)/(''k''<sub>0</sub>|'''r'''-'''r'''′|), with ''k''<sub>0</sub> = 2π/λ<sub>0</sub>. This matrix is [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian]] and its [[eigenvalue]]s Λ are [[Real number|real]]. For ''N'' points distributed randomly in a cube of side ''L'' and volume ''V'' = ''L''<sup>3</sup>, one can show<ref name=skipetrov11/> that the [[probability distribution]] of Λ is approximately given by the [[Marchenko–Pastur distribution|Marchenko-Pastur law]], if the density of points ρ = ''N''/''V'' obeys ρλ<sub>0</sub><sup>3</sup> ≤ 1 and 2.8''N''/(''k''<sub>0</sub> ''L'')<sup>2</sup> < 1 (see figure).

{{clear}}

[[File:Fig expc.png|thumb|340px|alt=Example 2 | Example of the probability distribution of eigenvalues Λ of the Euclidean random matrix generated by the function ''f''('''r''', '''r'''′) = exp(''ik''<sub>0</sub>ǀ'''r'''-'''r'''′ǀ)/(''k''<sub>0</sub>ǀ'''r'''-'''r'''′ǀ), with ''k''<sub>0</sub> = 2π/λ<sub>0</sub> and ''f''('''r'''= '''r'''′) = 0.]]

=== Non-Hermitian Euclidean random matrices ===

A theory for the [[eigenvalue]] density of large (''N''≫1) non-Hermitian Euclidean random matrices has been developed<ref name=goetschy11a>{{Cite journal | last1 = Goetschy | first1 = A. | last2 = Skipetrov | first2 = S. | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevE.84.011150 | title = Non-Hermitian Euclidean random matrix theory | journal = Physical Review E | volume = 84 | year = 2011 | issue = 1 | article-number = 011150 | pmid = 21867155 |arxiv = 1102.1850 |bibcode = 2011PhRvE..84a1150G | s2cid = 44717545 }}</ref> and has been applied to study the problem of [[random laser]].<ref name=goetschy11b>{{Cite journal | last1 = Goetschy | first1 = A. | last2 = Skipetrov | first2 = S. E. | doi = 10.1209/0295-5075/96/34005 | title = Euclidean matrix theory of random lasing in a cloud of cold atoms | journal = EPL | volume = 96 | issue = 3 | article-number = 34005 | year = 2011 |arxiv = 1104.2711 |bibcode = 2011EL.....9634005G | s2cid = 119116200 }}</ref>

''Example 2:'' Consider the matrix Â generated by the function ''f''('''r''', '''r'''′) = exp(''ik''<sub>0</sub>|'''r'''-'''r'''′|)/(''k''<sub>0</sub>|'''r'''-'''r'''′|), with ''k''<sub>0</sub> = 2π/λ<sub>0</sub> and ''f''('''r'''= '''r'''′) = 0. This matrix is not Hermitian and its eigenvalues Λ are [[Complex number|complex]]. The probability distribution of Λ can be found analytically<ref name=goetschy11a/> if the density of point ρ = ''N''/''V'' obeys ρλ<sub>0</sub><sup>3</sup> ≤ 1 and 9''N''/(8''k''<sub>0</sub> ''R'')<sup>2</sup> < 1 (see figure).
